Quail

KWAYL -- to shrink back or lose courage; picture knees buckling before a threat. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To quail is to shrink back as fear takes hold and courage fails.

Even seasoned reporters quail when the general fixes them with his icy stare.

Worked Example

As the towering wave rises over the small boat, the new deckhand's legs lock, his grip loosens, and he shrinks back against the cabin wall, unable to move.

That instinctive shrinking back in fear is exactly what it means to quail. Unlike 'flee,' which means running away, to quail is to freeze and shrink where you stand.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flinch: to make a small, startled recoil

cower: to crouch down in fear

recoil: to spring back in fear or disgust

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confront: to face someone or something boldly

withstand: to stand firm against pressure

Where it sits · how fully fear takes over — flinch → quail → cower

flinch vs. quail: Flinch is smaller and quicker than quail -- a flinch is a split-second twitch at a sudden threat, while to quail is to visibly lose courage in the face of it.

cower vs. quail: Cower is more physical and extreme than quail: to quail is to shrink back inwardly and hesitate, while to cower is to crouch and huddle in open, helpless fear.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — quail-

root — quail-: to give way, weaken (Middle English (quailen; origin uncertain, perhaps Middle Dutch quelen, 'to suffer'))

Put it together

Put it together: Quail entered Middle English as quailen, 'to give way or wither,' but its deeper origin is uncertain -- perhaps Middle Dutch quelen, 'to suffer.' It has no confirmed English relatives, though it keeps close company in meaning with words like wince and cower.

Use the root in a new word: wince

Use the root in a new word: wince: He couldn't help but wince when the dentist's drill started up.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Quail is a somewhat literary verb, usually followed by 'at' or 'before' -- crowds quail before a tyrant; a student might quail at the sight of the exam.
